reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Defined on high-resolution manometry (Chicago Classification) by premature (spastic) contractions with a shortened distal latency in at least 20% of swallows, with normal or near-normal lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation.

Presents with intermittent dysphagia to both solids and liquids and retrosternal chest pain that may closely mimic cardiac angina; symptoms are often unpredictable and precipitated by hot or cold liquids or emotional stress.
The classic 'corkscrew' or 'rosary bead' barium appearance reflects simultaneous non-peristaltic contractions but is seen in a minority and correlates poorly with symptoms.
Cardiac causes of chest pain must be excluded before attributing symptoms to oesophageal spasm, as the two are clinically indistinguishable at the bedside.
There is meaningful overlap with type III (spastic) achalasia; impaired LOS relaxation on manometry shifts the diagnosis toward achalasia rather than diffuse spasm.
Gastro-oesophageal reflux frequently coexists and may drive spastic motor activity, so an empirical trial of acid suppression is a reasonable early step.
Smooth-muscle relaxants (nitrates, calcium-channel blockers), and neuromodulators for visceral hypersensitivity are mainstays; peppermint oil can abolish simultaneous contractions.
Refractory cases may respond to endoscopic botulinum toxin injection or, rarely, to a long myotomy including peroral endoscopic myotomy tailored to the spastic segment.
reference.pathophysiology: Diffuse (distal) oesophageal spasm is a primary motor disorder of the oesophageal body characterised by loss of the normal orderly, sequential peristaltic wave in the smooth-muscle segment. The core defect is impaired deglutitive inhibition, attributed to dysfunction of inhibitory myenteric neurons that release nitric oxide; reduced nitrergic tone allows contractions to begin prematurely and propagate simultaneously rather than in an aboral sequence. This is reflected manometrically by a shortened distal latency. The resulting rapidly propagated or simultaneous contractions produce dysphagia and chest pain, and superimposed oesophageal hypersensitivity amplifies symptom perception. Unlike achalasia, lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation is typically preserved, though some patients show a spectrum bridging toward spastic achalasia.
additionalDifferentials: gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with reflux-induced chest pain
functional chest pain of presumed oesophageal origin
additionalInvestigations: high-resolution oesophageal manometry with distal latency measurement
timed barium oesophagram (may show corkscrew or segmental spasm)
upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsies to exclude mucosal and structural disease
ambulatory oesophageal pH-impedance monitoring to assess reflux contribution
cardiac assessment (ECG and stress or perfusion testing) to exclude ischaemia
provocative or pharmacological testing during manometry where available
functional lumen imaging probe (FLIP) to assess oesophagogastric junction distensibility
redFlags: progressive dysphagia, especially to solids, or significant weight loss suggesting stricture or malignancy
chest pain with cardiac risk factors or exertional pattern requiring urgent cardiac exclusion
food bolus impaction or inability to swallow saliva
onset in older patients over a short period, raising concern for pseudoachalasia from an infiltrating tumour
reference.prognosis: The condition is typically chronic and relapsing but benign, with symptoms fluctuating over years rather than progressing relentlessly; a substantial minority improve with reassurance, reflux control and neuromodulation. A subset evolve toward spastic achalasia over time, and response to invasive therapy is less predictable than in classic achalasia.
pitfalls: Attributing non-cardiac chest pain to spasm without first excluding coronary disease.
Over-reliance on the barium 'corkscrew' sign, which is neither sensitive nor specific and correlates poorly with symptoms.
Missing impaired lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation on manometry and thereby mislabelling type III achalasia as diffuse spasm.
Failing to recognise coexistent gastro-oesophageal reflux as a treatable driver of spastic activity.
Proceeding to a short myotomy without mapping the length of the spastic segment, risking incomplete symptom relief.
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease, current edition
Chicago Classification of Oesophageal Motility Disorders (current version)
ACG Clinical Guideline on oesophageal motility disorders
management: Exclude a cardiac cause of chest pain first, then reassure, as symptoms closely mimic angina
Empirical acid suppression with a proton pump inhibitor, since coexistent gastro-oesophageal reflux frequently drives spastic motor activity
Smooth-muscle relaxants such as nitrates or calcium channel blockers before meals to reduce premature contractions, with peppermint oil as an adjunct
Neuromodulation with a tricyclic antidepressant or similar pain modulator to dampen oesophageal hypersensitivity and chest pain
Trigger avoidance, including very hot or cold liquids, and stress-reduction strategies
Endoscopic botulinum toxin injection into the distal oesophagus for refractory symptoms
Reserve peroral endoscopic myotomy or Heller myotomy for disease that is refractory or evolving towards spastic (type III) achalasia
